overview.name: EcoGiro
overview.tagline: Designing the connection between citizens and recyclers.
overview.summary: In two months, I turned research on recycling in Bogotá into user flows and interface designs for a collection MVP. My work connected material preparation with the information recyclers need before accepting a pickup.

image.alt: EcoGiro Home screen with the scan action, 14 eco-points, no upcoming collections, recycling tips, and bottom navigation.

benefit.title: Recycle with confidence
benefit.description: I designed the journey around a practical question: what does each person need to know before handing over plastic? Preparation guidance sits after the scan. Material details travel with the collection request so recyclers can review it before responding.

problem.title: Preparation mistakes reach the recycler
paragraphs: Citizens need guidance on preparing plastic. Recyclers receive mixed material and discover its condition at pickup. I focused the design on that gap: the information missing between preparation at home and collection.

I synthesized the team’s field interview with Cecilia Gamboa, a recycler with ten years of experience, alongside secondary research from ReciRed Bogotá (Universidad EAN, 2025). Her account of sorting bags by hand exposed contamination and poorly packed glass. I translated those findings into preparation guidance and material information shown before a recycler accepts.
problem.question: How might we make preparing and handing over plastic simple for citizens, while giving recyclers the information and autonomy to collect it safely?

images.alt: Teach at the point of action. Knowing the recycling rules does not ensure correct separation. Give material-specific instructions immediately after the scan.
Make the handoff predictable. The interview highlighted contamination and missing information. Show material condition and risk notes before a recycler accepts.
Reduce the learning burden. Cecilia mainly used her phone for emergencies. A lightweight messaging flow was chosen as a hypothesis to test with recyclers.

paragraphs: I organized the citizen app into Home, Collections, Rewards, and Profile. Scanning starts from Home and leads through preparation to a collection request. This keeps the main task in one flow and makes active requests easy to find.

I separated requesting a pickup from confirming one. Citizens propose an address and time; recyclers can accept, decline, or suggest another time through Telegram. The pending state makes clear that sending a request does not guarantee collection.

The service map connects citizens, EcoGiro, recyclers, and collection centers. I kept center-side material validation and centralized payments in the roadmap so the MVP could focus on preparation and coordination.

User includes medals, scanning and scheduled collection, recoveries and recovery detail, rewards, and profile with FAQ and data policy. paragraphs: I gave scanning priority on Home and placed preparation guidance before scheduling. That sequence gives citizens the material information they need before committing to a collection request.

The wireframes keep the material summary visible while users enter collection details. I defined empty, pending, accepted, alternative-time, rejected, and collected states to cover the handoff beyond the ideal path.

items.title: One clear starting point
items.description: Keep the scan action prominent, with points and the next collection as supporting information.

items.title: Guidance before scheduling
items.description: Identify the material and explain cleaning, drying, flattening, and safe packing when applicable.

items.title: Confirmation is a distinct state
items.description: A sent request does not promise a pickup. Show the recycler response and let the citizen review an alternative time.

solution.subtitle: From a photo to a handoff
paragraphs: The MVP follows plastic from identification and preparation through the collection request and recycler response. I designed the supporting screens for profile details, contextual help, collection history, and reward progress around that journey.

features.title: Identify & prepare
paragraphs: I paired AI-assisted material identification with preparation instructions and visible uncertainty. When the image cannot confirm the resin, the result says so. This makes the limits of classification part of the experience.

features.title: Request & coordinate
features.benefit: People keep control of the handoff
paragraphs: The request carries the material summary, address, and proposed time. Recyclers receive the details through Telegram and choose how to respond. Channel adoption and the proposed 24-hour coordination window are priorities for the pilot.

features.title: Track & reward
paragraphs: I used collection status and history to show what happens after a request is sent. The reward concept links eco-points to completed deliveries. Partner offers and environmental impact conversions remain proposals to validate.

system.subtitle: A clear system for everyday actions
paragraphs: I brought the collection journey into a shared UI system with Poppins, Lucide React icons, and an 8-point spacing scale. The component specifications document dimensions and states for recurring actions such as scheduling, reviewing a request, and checking status.

foundations.title: Color
paragraphs: Green identifies primary actions; mint and cream separate content from the page. Coral supports destructive or error states, while light blue distinguishes active status. Labels and icons must carry the meaning alongside color.

foundations.title: Typography
paragraphs: I used Poppins with distinct weights and sizes for screen titles, material instructions, actions, and supporting details. The hierarchy gives preparation steps priority over secondary information.
A clear hierarchy helps people scan material details and understand the next step without relying only on color or icons.

foundations.title: Iconography
paragraphs: EcoGiro uses Lucide React icons for navigation, scanning, collection, profile, and support. The original SVG components share a consistent line weight and use the project green. Text labels accompany icons in the interface.

foundations.title: Buttons
paragraphs: Primary actions use full-width buttons. The specifications define focus, pressed, and disabled states, plus inline validation for errors. Accessibility checks remain part of the validation plan.

components.title: Components
components.introduction: The component specifications give the team a shared reference for collection, rewards, notifications, and location flows. Each example records dimensions and content states.
components.conclusion: These patterns connect the same material, address, and status information across scheduling, collection cards, and detail views.

outcome.title: Outcome & Reflection
outcome.subtitle: Research translated into an MVP and a pilot plan
paragraphs: Across the two-month project, I connected research synthesis with user flows, the sitemap, and contextual education for the MVP. My contribution gave the team a design rationale for what information to show before a request and how to represent the recycler’s response.

The business proposal focused on collection centers as a potential B2B customer for coordination and traceability. I considered how pickup quantities, route density, and material quality would affect the experience. Pricing and operating costs still need validation.

The project reached an MVP and a pilot plan. The next step is to test it in a small area with a collection center and a limited recycler group. Usability, classification accuracy, and environmental impact have not yet been measured.

learnings.title: Safety starts before pickup
learnings.description: The interview changed what I prioritized on the scan result: preparation steps and risk information. In a pilot, I would check whether those instructions lead to material arriving in better condition.

learnings.title: Coordination requires autonomy
learnings.description: I made the recycler’s response a distinct part of the flow. This decision applies to services where a customer request depends on another person’s availability and acceptance.

learnings.title: A useful flow needs viable operations
learnings.description: I connected interface decisions to pickup quantities, route density, and reward costs. Those constraints need to shape the pilot before the service expands.

metrics.title: Scan → request
metrics.description: Measure whether people understand the result and continue to a valid collection request.

metrics.title: Response → completed collection
metrics.description: Track recycler response time and the share of requests completed within the proposed window.

metrics.title: Quality & repeat use
metrics.description: Record validated kilograms, rejected or contaminated material, cost per kilogram, and a second collection within 30 days.

outcome.takeaway: I can help a product team turn field research into service flows, explicit states, and UI specifications that give engineering a concrete starting point.

0.title: Discovery
paragraphs: I structured the research questions and recycler interview guide, then synthesized the team’s interview and secondary research. Contamination and missing information became design priorities: preparation guidance after scanning and material details before pickup acceptance.

1.title: UX / Structure
paragraphs: I mapped the citizen, recycler, and collection-center journeys and defined the MVP sitemap. I separated sending a request from confirming collection and used Telegram as the proposed recycler channel. This gave the team a flow with explicit roles and response states.

image.alt: EcoGiro scan result with environmental guidance, an estimated weight labeled as not measured, and the schedule collection action.
image.caption: UX / Structure · From scan result to collection

2.title: UI Design
paragraphs: I translated the research into preparation guidance, a prominent scan action, and visible collection states. I documented recurring UI patterns so the same information and actions could stay consistent across screens.

image.alt: EcoGiro collection scheduling screen with a material summary, estimated weight, address, date, time slots, and an optional comment.
image.caption: UI Design · Collection scheduling

3.title: Validation plan
paragraphs: I defined a pilot around the assumptions that could block the service: understanding the scan result, responding through Telegram, and completing a viable pickup. The plan tracks request completion, response time, material quality, and cost per kilogram.
